reigns.tagline: The pagan king who carved Denmark's name in stone
reigns.cameToPower: Rose from Jutland chieftain to king
reigns.previously: Viking Age Denmark: raiders, warlords, and no lasting royal line.
paragraphs: Around 900, Denmark is a patchwork. Chieftains, sea raiders and petty kings fight over Jutland and the islands, while Viking fleets rob their way round Europe. Then a man called Gorm turns up at Jelling, in the middle of Jutland. Nobody knows quite where he came from. What he left behind is the start of a monarchy that still exists today, the oldest in Europe.

Gorm stuck to the old gods. A German churchman later called him a cruel enemy of Christians. But his best-known act is a tender one. He raised a runestone at Jelling for his wife Thyra and called her "Denmark's adornment". It's the oldest native record of the name Denmark. When he died, around 958, a huge burial mound went up at Jelling. His son Harald was already waiting to take over.

claims.text: Gorm's small Jelling stone is the first time Danes wrote the name "Denmark" at home.
claims.note: The runes say "tanmarkar" in Thyra's honour. Foreign writers had used the name earlier, but this is the oldest Danish use.

claims.text: Gorm swore to kill anyone who told him his favourite son was dead, so Thyra told him with mourning cloth instead.
claims.note: A saga and Saxo tale written over 200 years later. Good drama, no early evidence.

claims.text: Bones found under Jelling church in 1978 are Gorm's, moved there by his Christian son.
claims.note: The north mound's chamber is empty and dated to 958–59. The church skeleton fits, but nothing names it.

reigns.hook: The old king is in his mound. His son Harald has bigger plans: one Denmark, one king, and a new god to go with them.

reigns.tagline: The Viking king who went Christian and built big
reigns.previously: Gorm the Old is buried at Jelling. Harald takes over.
paragraphs: Harald took Gorm's patchy kingdom and nailed it down. Around 965 he was baptised and turned Denmark officially Christian. Then he raised a second, much bigger stone at Jelling. It shows Christ on one face and boasts that Harald won all of Denmark and Norway and "made the Danes Christian". It's sometimes called Denmark's birth certificate.

He was a builder too. Around 980 his men put up perfectly round ring forts, like Trelleborg on Zealand, and a long timber bridge at Ravning. He also had wars with the German emperor. Then his son Sweyn rebelled. Harald was wounded and fled to the Baltic coast, where he died around 986. A thousand years later, tech engineers named Bluetooth after him because he united rival groups.

claims.text: Harald converted after a priest called Poppo carried red-hot iron without being burned.
claims.note: Widukind of Corvey wrote this within a few years. Harald's conversion is real; the miracle is the shaky bit.

claims.text: He got the name Bluetooth from a dead, dark tooth.
claims.note: The nickname is old, but nobody knows what it meant. Dark-tooth is just one popular guess.

claims.text: The Bluetooth logo is made of Harald's initials in runes.
claims.note: The symbol joins the runes for H and B. The name was picked in the late 1990s as a stand-in and stuck.

reigns.hook: Harald is dead in exile, beaten by his own son. Sweyn Forkbeard has the crown, and he is already looking west across the sea at England.

reigns.tagline: Kicked out his father, then took England
reigns.previously: Harald Bluetooth dies in exile after his son's revolt.
paragraphs: Sweyn started his reign by beating his own father, and he never really stopped fighting. In 1000 he helped crush King Olaf Tryggvason of Norway at the sea battle of Svolder, and took a share of Norway as his prize. Through the 990s and 1000s his fleets raided England again and again, squeezing huge payments of silver out of King Æthelred.

In 1013 he stopped raiding and started conquering. He landed on the Humber, town after town gave in, and by Christmas Æthelred had fled to Normandy. Sweyn was the first Dane to be accepted as king of all England. He held it for about five weeks. On 3 February 1014 he died at Gainsborough, and the whole conquest was suddenly up for grabs.

claims.text: Sweyn was furious because his sister Gunhild died in the St Brice's Day massacre of Danes in England in 1002.
claims.note: The massacre is real, but Gunhild's death there is told only by much later writers.

claims.text: The ghost of St Edmund, the king the Vikings had martyred, struck Sweyn dead with a spear.
claims.note: A story from Bury St Edmunds, written to warn off anyone who taxed the abbey. Nobody at the time knew why he died.

claims.text: Sweyn was once captured and had to be ransomed.
claims.note: Thietmar of Merseburg and later saga writers mention it, but they disagree on who took him.

reigns.hook: Sweyn is dead and England is slipping away. In Denmark, his son Harald takes the throne, while his brother Cnut stays in England to fight.

reigns.tagline: The quiet brother who kept the home fires burning
reigns.cameToPower: Took Denmark when his father died
reigns.previously: Sweyn Forkbeard dies five weeks after winning England.
paragraphs: Harald II is one of the least known kings of Denmark. When Sweyn died in England in 1014, the Danish army there backed his son Cnut, but it was Harald who got Denmark. Cnut was soon chased out of England and sailed home with nothing. One source says he asked Harald to split the kingdom, and Harald said no.

So Cnut went back to England with a new army, and Harald seems to have helped him. The brothers are also said to have fetched their mother home from the Slav lands. By 1016 Cnut was king of England. Harald, meanwhile, simply fades out of the record. He died around 1018, apparently without children, and the brother who had wanted half of Denmark now got all of it.

claims.text: Cnut asked Harald to share Denmark and Harald turned him down.
claims.note: Only the Encomium Emmae Reginae tells this, and it was written about 25 years later to flatter Cnut's widow.

claims.text: Harald was the elder of the two brothers.
claims.note: The Encomium seems to say so, but other sources are unclear and historians still argue.

reigns.hook: Harald is gone. Cnut, already king of England, now adds Denmark. He's about to build an empire across the North Sea.

reigns.tagline: Emperor of the North Sea
reigns.previously: Harald II dies quietly, leaving no children.
paragraphs: Cnut had already won England in 1016. He married Æthelred's widow, Emma of Normandy, so the English got the same queen back. Then Denmark fell to him when his brother died. He ruled from England mostly, with trusted earls in charge back home, and kept the peace with heavy taxes, a big standing fleet and a lot of shrewd charm.

In 1026 he fought a Norwegian and Swedish alliance at the Holy River, and afterwards had his own brother-in-law Ulf killed in a Roskilde church. In 1027 he walked in Rome at the crowning of the German emperor. By 1028 he had chased King Olaf out of Norway. He died at Shaftesbury in 1035, and his empire started coming apart at once.

claims.text: Cnut sat on the beach and ordered the tide to stop, to show his courtiers that even kings can't command the sea.
claims.note: First told by Henry of Huntingdon about 100 years later. In his version Cnut is being humble, not foolish.

claims.text: Ulf was killed after quarrelling with Cnut over a game of chess.
claims.note: Snorri's saga, two centuries on. Ulf's killing is accepted; the chess quarrel is storytelling.

claims.text: Cnut went to Rome in 1027 and saw Emperor Conrad II crowned.
claims.note: Cnut says so himself in a letter to the English, and other writers back him up.

reigns.hook: Cnut is dead. His son Harthacnut holds Denmark, but England is grabbed by his half-brother Harold, and Norway has broken free.

reigns.tagline: Last Danish king of England, killed by a toast
reigns.previously: Cnut the Great dies, and his empire splits at once.
paragraphs: Harthacnut was Cnut's son by Emma, and he should have had England too. But Denmark was under threat from young King Magnus of Norway, so he stayed home, and his half-brother Harold Harefoot took the English crown. The two northern kings finally cut a deal: whoever died first, the other got his kingdom.

When Harold died in 1040, Harthacnut sailed to England with a war fleet. One of his first acts was to have Harold's body dug up and thrown away. He taxed so hard that Worcester rioted. Then, in June 1042, at a wedding feast at Lambeth, he stood up with his drink, fell down in a fit and never spoke again. He was only in his twenties.

claims.text: Harthacnut died with a drink in his hand at a wedding.
claims.note: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says he was standing at his drink when he fell to the ground in convulsions.

claims.text: He was poisoned.
claims.note: Nothing at the time says so. A stroke or seizure fits the account just as well.

claims.text: He and Magnus agreed that each would inherit the other's kingdom.
claims.note: The deal comes from Norse sagas written later. Magnus certainly acted as if it existed.

reigns.hook: Harthacnut is dead and has no son. England picks his half-brother Edward. But in Norway, Magnus says the deal makes Denmark his.

reigns.tagline: The Norwegian boy king who won Denmark by a deal
reigns.previously: Harthacnut drops dead at a wedding feast, with no heir.
paragraphs: Magnus was the son of St Olaf, the Norwegian king Cnut had driven out. He grew up in exile in Russia and was brought home as a boy to be king of Norway. Now, thanks to his deal with Harthacnut, he claimed Denmark too, and the Danes accepted him. He made Sweyn Estridsen, Cnut's nephew, his earl there. Sweyn soon turned on him.

In 1043 Magnus smashed a huge Wendish army at Lyrskov Heath near Hedeby, one of the bloodiest fights of the age. He spent the next years chasing Sweyn round Denmark and had to share Norway with his uncle Harald Hardrada. He died in Denmark in 1047, still young. On his deathbed he is said to have given Denmark to Sweyn and Norway to Harald.

claims.text: St Olaf appeared to his son in a dream before Lyrskov Heath and promised him victory.
claims.note: Told in the sagas written two centuries later. The battle and the win are real; the dream is saga stuff.

claims.text: Magnus fought at Lyrskov with his father's axe, Hel.
claims.note: Snorri names the axe. It's a great detail with nothing earlier behind it.

claims.text: Dying, he split his kingdoms between his enemy Sweyn and his uncle Harald.
claims.note: The sagas say so. Harald Hardrada ignored it and fought Sweyn for Denmark for years.

reigns.hook: Magnus is dead. Sweyn, the earl who kept losing battles, is finally king. But Harald Hardrada wants Denmark too.

reigns.tagline: Lost every battle, won the kingdom, fathered kings
reigns.previously: Magnus dies, and Denmark passes to his rival Sweyn.
paragraphs: Sweyn's mother Estrid was Cnut's sister, and his father was Earl Ulf, the man Cnut had killed. He spent his first years as king fighting Harald Hardrada, who raided Denmark and burned Hedeby. Sweyn lost most of the battles but never gave up, and in 1064 Harald finally made peace. Two years later Harald died in England.

Sweyn was clever and liked talking. The German chronicler Adam of Bremen visited him and took much of his knowledge of the North from the king's own stories. Sweyn set up a network of bishoprics and sent a fleet to England in 1069 to test William the Conqueror. He also had a huge family, with many sons by several women. Five of them became king, one after another.

claims.text: Adam of Bremen got much of his information on Scandinavia straight from Sweyn.
claims.note: Adam says so himself, more than once, in his history written about 1075.

claims.text: Bishop William of Roskilde blocked the church door to Sweyn after the king had men killed there, and made him do penance.
claims.note: Saxo tells it over a century later. Sweyn and William were real friends, but the scene is shaped like a sermon.

claims.text: Five of his sons became king of Denmark.
claims.note: Harald, Cnut, Olaf, Eric and Niels all reigned. Most were born outside marriage.

reigns.hook: Sweyn is dead and he left a crowd of sons. Who gets the crown? The Danes will choose, and they pick the gentle one, Harald.

reigns.tagline: The soft king the Danes picked over his tough brother

start.note: On Sweyn II's death; the year is sometimes given as 1074

reigns.previously: Sweyn II dies, leaving a crowd of sons and no clear heir.
paragraphs: When Sweyn died, the Danes met at a Thing, an assembly, at Isøre on Zealand to pick his successor. The obvious fighter was his son Cnut. They chose Cnut's elder half-brother Harald instead, a mild man who promised to leave them alone. Cnut went off in a sulk, and some say to Sweden.

Harald kept his word. He's remembered for laws that eased old customs, and the medieval writers who disliked him called him lazy and weak. His nickname "Hen" may mean soft or limp. His reign was quiet and short. He died in April 1080, still fairly young, and was buried at Dalby in Scania. Brother Cnut was waiting.

claims.text: His nickname "Hen" meant he was soft or feeble.
claims.note: The word's meaning is uncertain; it may come from a whetstone. Later writers liked to paint him as weak.

claims.text: Harald was buried at Dalby church in Scania.
claims.note: Medieval tradition says so, and a niche in Dalby church is pointed out as his grave, but no remains have been identified.

reigns.hook: Gentle Harald is gone. The Danes turn to the brother they passed over, Cnut, a hard man with big plans for England.

reigns.tagline: The king who planned to take England and got killed
reigns.reignEnded: Killed in a church in Odense
reigns.previously: Harald Hen dies after four quiet years.
paragraphs: Cnut IV wanted to be his great-uncle Cnut the Great. He backed the Church, gave it land, and pushed royal rights hard: wrecks, unclaimed land and new fines all went to the crown. In 1085 he gathered a vast fleet in the Limfjord to invade England, with help from Norway and from his father-in-law, the count of Flanders. England panicked.

Then nothing happened. Trouble on the German border kept Cnut in the south, and the bored army went home. Cnut fined the men who had left, and Jutland rose in revolt. He fled to Odense and took refuge in St Alban's church. On 10 July 1086 rebels broke in and killed him at the altar, with his brother Benedict. Within 15 years the Pope had made him a saint.

claims.text: Cnut's invasion threat is one reason William the Conqueror ordered the Domesday survey.
claims.note: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle puts the scare and the survey side by side. Historians argue over how far one caused the other.

claims.text: Cnut was killed by a spear through his side as he knelt at the altar.
claims.note: Ælnoth's account, written to promote the saint, echoes Christ's death. The killing in the church is solid.

claims.text: His bones are still in Odense Cathedral.
claims.note: A skeleton in a shrine there has long been identified as Cnut's, with wounds that fit a violent death.

reigns.hook: The king is dead on the church floor. The crown goes to the brother many blamed for the trouble, Olaf, and the harvests are about to fail.

reigns.tagline: Nine years of famine, and the king took the blame
reigns.cameToPower: Freed from Flanders to be king
reigns.previously: Cnut IV is killed at the altar of St Alban's church, Odense.
paragraphs: Olaf was in prison when he became king. Cnut had suspected him of stirring up trouble and sent him to be held in Flanders. After Cnut's murder, the Danes chose Olaf, and their brother Niels was swapped in as a hostage to get him home. It wasn't a lucky start.

It got worse. Harvests failed year after year, and people went hungry across Denmark. Olaf got the nickname "Hunger". Plenty of Danes decided this was God punishing them for killing Cnut, the new martyr. Olaf died in August 1095, and nobody now knows where he is buried. His brother Eric, a much more popular man, took over.

claims.text: The famine was God's punishment for murdering Cnut.
claims.note: That was the Church's line, pushed by Ælnoth and later Saxo to boost Cnut's sainthood.

claims.text: Olaf offered to take the famine's guilt on himself so his people could be spared.
claims.note: A late tradition. Saxo is mostly hostile to Olaf and doesn't make him a hero.

claims.text: Denmark really did suffer a run of bad harvests under Olaf.
claims.note: Several medieval writers record it, though the details are thin and the scale is hard to judge.

reigns.hook: Olaf Hunger is dead and the famine is lifting. The new king is his brother Eric, big, cheerful and loved, but with a temper.

reigns.tagline: The well-loved king who died on the road to Jerusalem
reigns.previously: Olaf Hunger dies after nine years of bad harvests.
paragraphs: After the famine years, Eric felt like a fresh start. The good harvests came back, and people gave him the nickname "Evergood". He fought Wendish pirates on the Baltic coast and worked hard for the Church. He got the Pope to make his brother Cnut a saint in 1101. He also pushed for Denmark to get its own archbishop at Lund, free of the German church at Hamburg-Bremen.

He had a temper, though. After killing men at a feast, he swore to go to Jerusalem to atone. In 1103 he set off with his wife, Queen Bodil, travelling through Russia and Constantinople. He fell ill and died at Paphos on Cyprus that July. Bodil went on to the Holy Land and died there. Denmark was left without a king.

claims.text: Eric was the first Scandinavian king to set out on pilgrimage to Jerusalem.
claims.note: Danish historians often say so, but early sources are thin and it depends on how you count.

claims.text: He went because he had killed men at a feast in a rage.
claims.note: Saxo gives this reason, writing a century later. The pilgrimage itself is well recorded.

claims.text: Lund became an archbishopric thanks to Eric's lobbying.
claims.note: Eric met the Pope in Italy and the new archbishopric was set up right after his death.

reigns.hook: Eric is buried far from home in Cyprus. Back in Denmark, his brother Niels, the last of Sweyn's sons, waits to be chosen.

reigns.tagline: Thirty years on the throne, undone by one murder
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen king after Eric I died abroad
reigns.reignEnded: Cut down by the people of Schleswig
reigns.previously: Eric Evergood dies on Cyprus, a pilgrim far from home, in 1103.
paragraphs: Niels was the fourth son of Sweyn Estridsen to wear the crown, and he wore it for thirty years. He was steady rather than brilliant. His wife, Margaret Fredkulla, a Swedish king's daughter, was a big presence at court, and their son Magnus grew up expecting to be king next.

The problem was his nephew Cnut Lavard, Duke of Schleswig, who was rich, popular and German-polished. In January 1131 Magnus lured Cnut into a forest near Ringsted and killed him. Civil war followed. In June 1134, at Fotevik in Scania, Magnus died along with five bishops. Niels fled to Schleswig, Cnut Lavard's town. Its guild, which Cnut had led, shut the gates behind him and killed him.

claims.text: Niels knew of his son's plan to kill Cnut Lavard.
claims.note: Saxo hints the old king turned a blind eye, but nobody at the time proved he gave the order.

claims.text: Coins from his reign name Queen Margaret alongside the king.
claims.note: Surviving coins carry both names; numismatists call it a rare case of a medieval Scandinavian queen on coinage.

claims.text: Niels was warned not to enter Schleswig and went anyway.
claims.note: Saxo tells it as a tragic blunder; it reads like a moral story more than a report.

reigns.hook: Fotevik was won by Cnut Lavard's half-brother Eric, a man with a hard reputation. The old king is dead, his heir is dead, and Eric is now the obvious choice.

reigns.tagline: The avenger who was speared at a public assembly
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Nephew of Niels; son of Eric I
reigns.cameToPower: Won the civil war at Fotevik
reigns.previously: Old King Niels is killed by the townsmen of Schleswig.
paragraphs: Eric was an illegitimate son of Eric Evergood, and he had built his revenge for Cnut Lavard into a crown. At Fotevik he had a band of German mounted knights, which helped him crush Magnus. Once king, he got rid of rivals the blunt way. His own half-brother Harald Kesja and several of Harald's sons were put to death in 1135.

He also led a fleet against the pagan Wends on the island of Rügen. At home, though, people feared him more than they loved him. In September 1137 he was presiding over the Thing at Urnehoved in southern Jutland when a man known as Sorte Plov, “Black Plough”, stepped up and ran him through with a spear. His nickname Emune means “the Memorable”, and nobody forgot him in a hurry.

claims.text: German knights at Fotevik made it one of the first battles in Scandinavia decided by heavy cavalry.
claims.note: The Roskilde Chronicle and Saxo mention the knights; how decisive they were is a modern argument.

claims.text: His killer, Sorte Plov, acted out of personal revenge.
claims.note: Saxo gives him a grudge, but the motives of the killing are not clear in the early sources.

claims.text: Eric forced the people of Rügen to accept baptism in 1136.
claims.note: Saxo claims it; the conversion, if it happened, did not last.

reigns.hook: The killer has struck in front of the whole assembly. Eric's son Sweyn is a boy, so the magnates turn to a gentler choice: Eric Evergood's grandson, a young man nobody fears.

reigns.tagline: The gentle king who gave up his crown for a monk's habit
reigns.previously: Eric the Memorable is speared to death at the Urnehoved Thing.
paragraphs: Eric III was a grandson of Eric Evergood through his mother, and he was everything his uncle had not been. Mild, pious and sickly, he earned the nickname “the Lamb”. Strong men took advantage. A rival, Oluf, son of the murdered Harald Kesja, grabbed Scania and called himself king until he was killed in 1143.

Eric leaned hard on the Church and gave land to monasteries. By 1146 he was ill and worn out. He laid down the crown and entered St Canute's Abbey in Odense as a monk, and died there that summer. He left no son, and three different men looked at the empty throne and decided it was theirs.

claims.text: Eric III was the only Danish monarch to abdicate of his own free will until Margrethe II in 2024.
claims.note: Danish historians single him out this way; others who lost the crown were deposed.

claims.text: He was too weak to rule and the nobles ran the country.
claims.note: This is Saxo's verdict, written for the Valdemar kings, who had reasons to make this era look chaotic.

reigns.hook: Zealand cheers for Sweyn, son of Eric the Memorable. Jutland picks Cnut, son of the murderer Magnus. And Cnut Lavard's son Valdemar is growing up, watching both of them.

reigns.tagline: The emperor's man who threw a feast and a massacre
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Eric II, cousin of Eric III
reigns.previously: Eric the Lamb gives up his crown and dies a monk in Odense.
paragraphs: Sweyn was the son of Eric the Memorable and a mistress called Tunna. When Eric the Lamb walked away from the throne in 1146, Zealand and Scania shouted Sweyn king. Jutland picked his rival Cnut instead. For six years the two of them fought up and down the country, and young Valdemar, son of the murdered Cnut Lavard, backed Sweyn and was made Duke of Schleswig for it.

In 1152 Sweyn played his trump card. At Merseburg he knelt to Frederick Barbarossa, took his crown from the emperor's hand and became his vassal. Cnut had to give up the title of king. But Sweyn ruled hard, taxed hard and drove his friends away. Valdemar switched to Cnut, and in 1154 Sweyn fled to his wife's father in Saxony.

He was back by 1157 with German help, and the nobles brokered a deal: Denmark split three ways, sealed with a feast at Roskilde on 9 August. Sweyn's men burst in. Cnut died, Valdemar got away wounded. On 23 October the armies met at Grathe Heath near Viborg. Sweyn's side broke and he was killed as he ran. The heath gave him his nickname.

claims.text: Sweyn did homage to Frederick Barbarossa at Merseburg in 1152 and received his crown from him.
claims.note: German chroniclers, above all Otto of Freising, record the ceremony.

claims.text: Sweyn planned the Roskilde massacre before the feast began.
claims.note: Saxo paints it as cold treachery, but he wrote for Valdemar's family and Sweyn's side of the story is lost.

claims.text: Sweyn's horse got stuck in a bog and peasants finished him off with axes.
claims.note: A humiliating end told by Saxo, who had every reason to make Sweyn look bad.

reigns.hook: That's Sweyn's version. Over in Jutland, the man he fought for eleven years has his own story: Cnut, grandson of King Niels, whose father killed Valdemar's father.

reigns.tagline: The killer's son who made peace and died at dinner
reigns.previously: Eric the Lamb abdicates. Zealand hails Sweyn; Jutland wants Cnut.
paragraphs: Cnut came with baggage. His father was Magnus the Strong, who had murdered Cnut Lavard in 1131 and died at Fotevik three years later. His mother Richeza was a Polish princess. In 1146 the men of Jutland made him king to block Sweyn, and the two spent years at war. In 1147 they even joined the crusade against the pagan Wends side by side, and quarrelled the whole way.

At Merseburg in 1152 the emperor backed Sweyn. Cnut gave up the title of king and got lands on Zealand to keep him quiet. But Sweyn soon wore out his welcome. Valdemar, son of the man Cnut's father had killed, came over to Cnut's side, and the old feud was buried with a wedding: Valdemar was betrothed to Sophia, Cnut's half-sister. When Sweyn fled in 1154, Cnut and Valdemar shared Denmark.

Sweyn came back, and in 1157 the three agreed to split the kingdom. They sealed it with a feast in Roskilde on 9 August. Sweyn's men struck during the party. Cnut was cut down at the table. Valdemar was wounded and escaped into the dark.

claims.text: At Merseburg in 1152 Cnut gave up the name of king in return for lands.
claims.note: Otto of Freising, writing for Barbarossa, records the deal; Danish sources agree Sweyn came away as sole king.

claims.text: Valdemar married Cnut's half-sister Sophia to seal their alliance.
claims.note: Sophia was Richeza's daughter by her second husband, a Russian prince. She became Valdemar's queen.

reigns.hook: Valdemar got out of Roskilde alive and bleeding. Ten weeks later he meets Sweyn at Grathe Heath, and only one of them will leave it. Denmark is about to have a single king again.

reigns.tagline: The survivor who rebuilt Denmark with a fighting bishop
reigns.previously: Cnut dies at Roskilde, Sweyn at Grathe Heath. Valdemar stands alone.
paragraphs: Valdemar was born a week after his father's murder and raised alongside Absalon, a tough, clever noble boy who became his right hand. Absalon was made Bishop of Roskilde in 1158 and spent the next decades in armour. Together they hit back at the Wendish pirates who had been raiding Danish coasts for years.

In 1168 they took Arkona on Rügen and chopped up the giant four-headed idol of the god Svantevit. Absalon built a castle at a fishing village called Havn, the start of Copenhagen. In 1170, in Ringsted, Valdemar had his father enshrined as a saint and his seven-year-old son Cnut crowned on the same day. The message was clear. The crown now belonged to his line.

claims.text: Absalon founded Copenhagen in 1167.
claims.note: 1167 is the traditional date, taken from Absalon's castle. Archaeology shows a settlement there before him.

claims.text: The Danes chopped up Svantevit's idol and used it as firewood to cook their dinner.
claims.note: The vivid scene comes from Saxo, writing decades later for Absalon; it may be polished for effect.

claims.text: Saxo's history was written to glorify Valdemar and Absalon.
claims.note: Saxo worked for Absalon and says so; historians read him with that in mind.

reigns.hook: Valdemar dies in 1182. His son Cnut, crowned as a boy twelve years earlier, now rules alone. Within weeks a messenger arrives from the German emperor with a demand.

reigns.previously: Valdemar the Great dies at Vordingborg, his son already crowned.
paragraphs: Frederick Barbarossa wanted the new young king to kneel and take Denmark as an imperial fief, as Sweyn III once had. Cnut refused. The emperor set Duke Bogislaw of Pomerania on him, and in 1184 Absalon's fleet smashed Bogislaw's ships. The duke ended up as Denmark's vassal, and Cnut called himself King of the Danes and the Wends.

There was trouble in the family too. His cousin Bishop Valdemar of Schleswig plotted for the throne and spent years locked up. Cnut's sister Ingeborg married King Philip II of France in 1193, and Philip rejected her the morning after the wedding. Cnut and his brother Valdemar seized Holstein. Cnut died in 1202 with no children, and his brother took over.

claims.text: Philip II rejected Ingeborg the day after the wedding.
claims.note: French and papal records describe the scandal, which dragged on for twenty years.

claims.text: Absalon, not Cnut, really ran Denmark.
claims.note: Saxo's history makes Absalon the hero, so it's hard to tell how much the king decided himself.

reigns.hook: His younger brother Valdemar is 32, already the conqueror of Holstein, and he's got huge plans for the Baltic.

reigns.tagline: A flag from the sky, a kidnapping and a famous law code
reigns.previously: Cnut VI dies childless; his brother Valdemar inherits.
paragraphs: Valdemar built a Baltic empire. He ruled Holstein and Lübeck, and in 1219 he sailed to Estonia. At Lyndanisse, the future Tallinn, his camp was attacked and the battle turned his way. Then on Lyø island in 1223, Count Henry of Schwerin grabbed him and his eldest son while they slept and dragged them off to Germany.

He bought his freedom in 1225 for a huge ransom and most of his German lands. He tried to win them back and lost at Bornhöved in 1227. At home he did better. In March 1241 he gave Denmark the Code of Jutland, which starts “With law shall the land be built”. He died weeks later. His eldest son had died hunting, so three more sons were waiting.

claims.text: The Dannebrog fell from the sky during the battle at Lyndanisse.
claims.note: The story first appears around 300 years later, in the 1520s, in writings by Danish friars.

claims.text: The Dannebrog is the oldest national flag still in use.
claims.note: A popular Danish claim; it depends on how you define a national flag.

claims.text: The Code of Jutland stayed in force in parts of Schleswig until 1900.
claims.note: It was only replaced there when the German civil code arrived in 1900.

reigns.hook: Valdemar's sons are Eric, Abel and Christopher. Eric gets the crown, Abel gets Schleswig, and the two can't stand each other.

reigns.reignEnded: Beheaded; body dumped in the Schlei
reigns.previously: Valdemar the Victorious dies, weeks after giving Denmark its law.
paragraphs: Eric spent his reign at war with his own brother. Abel, Duke of Schleswig, wanted to run his duchy like a separate country, and the Church wanted its taxes left alone. To pay for his armies Eric charged a tax on every plough, which earned him a nickname he probably didn't want. The farmers of Scania rose against it.

In August 1250 Eric visited Abel in Schleswig, apparently to make peace. His brother's men seized him, rowed him out on the Schlei fjord and cut off his head. They weighed the body with chains and sank it. Fishermen found it later. Abel swore with two dozen nobles that he had nothing to do with it, and the magnates made him king.

claims.text: Abel ordered his brother's murder.
claims.note: The annals point straight at him, and nobody believed his oath, but there's no proof of a direct order.

claims.text: Eric's body was found by fishermen and miracles followed.
claims.note: A local cult grew up around 'Saint Eric', but the Church never made him a saint.

reigns.hook: Abel swears he is innocent, and the crown is his. But people are whispering, and Abel's luck is running out faster than anyone guesses.

reigns.tagline: The brother-killer who didn't rest in peace
reigns.previously: Eric Ploughpenny is beheaded on the Schlei. All eyes are on Abel.
paragraphs: Abel was crowned at Roskilde on 1 November 1250, but he never escaped the shadow of his brother's death. He got to work quickly, settling quarrels with the Church and trying to raise new taxes. One of those taxes was the problem.

In 1252 he marched against the Frisian farmers of the North Sea marshes, who refused to pay. Near Husum the Frisians caught his army at a river crossing and he was killed. His eldest son Valdemar was stuck in Germany, a prisoner of the Archbishop of Cologne, picked up on his way home from his studies. So the crown jumped to the youngest brother, Christopher.

claims.text: Abel's ghost rides through the woods near Schleswig with a pack of black hounds.
claims.note: Folk tales from Schleswig, told long after his death, say his body was moved to a bog and staked down.

claims.text: A Frisian wheelwright struck the fatal blow.
claims.note: Later chronicles name the killer; the early annals just say he fell in battle.

reigns.hook: Christopher, the last of Valdemar II's sons, takes the throne. His real opponent will be the Church, led by a stubborn archbishop of Lund.

reigns.cameToPower: Elected while Abel's son was jailed
reigns.previously: King Abel falls in battle against the Frisian farmers.
paragraphs: Christopher's big fight was with Jakob Erlandsen, Archbishop of Lund. Jakob believed the Church answered only to Rome and wanted to keep the crown out of its business. In 1256 the bishops declared that if any of them was arrested, the whole country would go under interdict, with no masses and no burials.

Christopher called his bluff. In 1259 he had the archbishop arrested and locked up, and the interdict came down. Weeks later, at Ribe, the king suddenly died. People said a church abbot had poisoned his communion wine. He left a ten-year-old son, Eric, and a formidable widow, Margaret Sambiria, who would fight to keep the crown in the family.

claims.text: Christopher was poisoned with communion wine by Abbot Arnfast of Ry.
claims.note: The rumour circulated after his death. Nothing proves it; a sudden illness is just as likely.

claims.text: The arrested archbishop was paraded in a fool's hat.
claims.note: A colourful story repeated by later writers; the early sources simply record his imprisonment.

reigns.hook: The new king is ten years old. His mother is in charge, Abel's sons want the crown back, and the archbishop is still locked up.

reigns.cameToPower: Inherited as a boy; mother regent
reigns.previously: Christopher I dies suddenly at Ribe. Poison is the talk of the town.
paragraphs: Eric's childhood was rough. In 1261 his mother's army lost at Lohede to Abel's family and their German allies, and the boy king was taken prisoner. He spent years as a captive in Brandenburg and came home engaged to a Brandenburg princess. As an adult he kept fighting nobles, bishops and his Schleswig cousins.

In 1282 the magnates made him sign a charter. He had to meet them every year and could not imprison a man without a trial. On the night of 22 November 1286 he was asleep in a barn at Finderup, near Viborg, when armed men burst in. They stabbed him 56 times. A court later blamed nine nobles, led by the marshal, Stig Andersen.

claims.text: The 1282 charter was Denmark's first constitution.
claims.note: It's often called that, but it was a deal with the nobles, not a constitution in the modern sense.

claims.text: Marshal Stig killed the king because Eric had seduced his wife.
claims.note: It's the plot of the medieval Marsk Stig ballads; no early source says so.

claims.text: The nine outlawed nobles were innocent.
claims.note: Their trial was rushed, and historians still argue over who really planned the murder.

reigns.hook: The killers flee to Norway, and Eric's 12-year-old son is king. Before long the outlaws are back on an island fortress, minting fake coins and raiding the coast.

reigns.previously: Eric Klipping is murdered in a barn. Nine nobles are outlawed.
paragraphs: Eric came to the throne as a boy with his mother Agnes in charge. The outlaws of Finderup set up a fortress on the island of Hjelm with Norwegian help, raiding Danish coasts and minting counterfeit coins. Then he fell out with Archbishop Jens Grand, threw him in prison, and got the Pope down on his head.

Eric wanted to be a big player in northern Germany. He threw lavish knighting festivals at Rostock and fought expensive wars. To pay for it, he taxed hard and mortgaged castles and whole regions to German lords. When Jutland's farmers revolted he crushed them and made them build his castles. When he died in 1319, none of his children had lived.

claims.text: The nickname Menved came from his habit of swearing “by all holy men”.

claims.text: Eric and his queen Ingeborg had many children, and none survived.
claims.note: Chronicles list several pregnancies and early deaths; the line ended with him.

reigns.hook: Eric is gone, and so is most of the treasury. The only heir is his brother Christopher, who once rebelled against him. The nobles will let him rule, but only on their terms.

reigns.cameToPower: Elected after signing a strict charter

reigns.previously: Eric Menved dies childless, leaving debts everywhere.
paragraphs: Christopher got the crown only after signing a tough charter in 1320 that tied his hands on taxes, wars and justice. He broke it, and his creditors, the counts of Holstein, lost patience. In 1326 the nobles and Count Gerhard III threw him out and put a boy, Duke Valdemar of Schleswig, on the throne instead.

Christopher came back in 1329 with help from Gerhard's cousin, Count John. But the price was the whole kingdom. Danish provinces were handed to the two counts as security for loans the crown could never repay. When he died at Nykøbing Falster in 1332, Christopher owned almost nothing. Denmark had no real king.

claims.text: By 1332 the entire country was pledged to German counts.
claims.note: Charters and chronicles show Jutland, Funen, Zealand and Scania in pawn; Scania then went to Sweden's king.

claims.text: The 1320 charter was the harshest any Danish king had signed.
claims.note: Historians see it as a turning point in noble power over the crown, but "harshest" is a judgement call; Eric V's charter of 1282 came first.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 1326. With Christopher on the run, Count Gerhard needs a king he can steer. He has one at home: his nephew Valdemar, the boy Duke of Schleswig.

reigns.previously: Christopher breaks his charter. His Holstein creditors want him out.
paragraphs: Valdemar became Duke of Schleswig at about 11, when his father died in 1325. His guardian was his mother's brother, Count Gerhard III of Holstein. In 1326 Gerhard and the Danish nobles rose against Christopher II, who fled to Germany. The magnates needed a king who would do as he was told, and they chose the boy duke, a descendant of King Abel.

The price was paid in Schleswig. Gerhard was given the duchy as a hereditary fief, and a pledge known as the Constitutio Valdemariana said Schleswig and the Danish crown must never again be held by the same man. Gerhard ran the government. Danish lords helped themselves to castles and lands. Valdemar had a royal seal and very little else.

The arrangement soured fast. In 1329 Gerhard's cousin, Count John, brought Christopher back. A deal was struck: Valdemar gave up the crown and went home to Schleswig as duke, and Gerhard took Jutland and Funen in pawn instead. Valdemar ruled Schleswig until his death in 1364, and in 1340 his sister Helvig married Christopher's son, the future Valdemar IV.

claims.text: In 1326 the crown promised that Schleswig and Denmark would never again share a ruler.
claims.note: No 1326 text survives: the clause is known only because Christian I quoted it in a pledge of 1448. Most historians accept it, and it fed the Schleswig question for centuries.

claims.text: Valdemar was only a puppet of his uncle Gerhard.
claims.note: He was a boy, and historians agree Gerhard held the real power; the records show the count as regent.

reigns.hook: Back on the throne, Christopher owns almost nothing. When he dies in 1332, nobody bothers to choose a new king. Denmark belongs to its creditors, and the biggest of them is the Bald Count.

reigns.title: The Kingless Time
reigns.tagline: Eight years with no king and a country in hock
reigns.cameToPower: Held the kingdom in pawn for debts
reigns.previously: Christopher II dies in 1332, broke, with his kingdom pawned away.
paragraphs: When Christopher II died in 1332, nobody bothered to choose a new king. There was hardly anything left to rule. Almost every province had been pawned to German lords as security for royal debts. Count Gerhard III of Holstein held Jutland and Funen. His cousin John held Zealand. Skåne threw off its Holstein masters and went over to the King of Sweden, who paid off the debt.

Gerhard, nicknamed the Bald Count, was the real boss of Denmark. He was a hard soldier and a harder landlord, and his German troops squeezed the Danes for every penny. In 1340 he marched into Jutland with a big army to stamp out unrest there, and set up his quarters in the town of Randers.

In the night of 1 April 1340, a Jutland squire named Niels Ebbesen slipped into Randers with a small band, burst in on Gerhard and killed him. Ebbesen got away and became a folk hero almost overnight, though he was himself killed fighting Holstein troops later that year. With the Bald Count gone, the Danes finally had room to pick a king.

claims.text: Niels Ebbesen killed the Bald Count at Randers in the night of 1 April 1340.
claims.note: Danish and north German chronicles of the 1300s record the killing; the date is the generally accepted one.

claims.text: Ebbesen was a patriot striking a blow to free Denmark from the Germans.
claims.note: That's how later ballads and 19th-century nationalists told it. Some historians think a quarrel between Ebbesen and the count mattered just as much.

claims.text: In the ballad, Ebbesen refuses to serve the count to his face, then comes back by night to kill him.
claims.note: The folk ballad of Niels Ebbesen was written down long after the event and is drama, not reporting.

reigns.hook: The Danes turn to Christopher II's youngest son, Valdemar, who grew up in exile at the German emperor's court. He has a claim and not a penny. He's going to buy his country back, one castle at a time.

reigns.tagline: The king who bought his country back
reigns.cameToPower: Elected after the Bald Count's murder
reigns.previously: Niels Ebbesen kills the Bald Count. Denmark is up for grabs.
paragraphs: Valdemar grew up in exile at the German emperor's court and came home in 1340 with a claim and empty pockets. He married Helvig of Schleswig and took a slice of North Jutland as her dowry. Then he got to work. He taxed, haggled, sold Estonia to the Teutonic Knights in 1346 and used the cash to buy back castles and provinces one by one. Where money wouldn't do it, he used force.

By 1360 he had most of the kingdom back, Skåne included. He wasn't finished. In 1361 he sailed to Gotland, cut down a peasant army outside Visby and made the rich trading town pay up. That was too much for the Hanseatic League, the German trading cities that ran the Baltic. They went to war, and by 1368 Valdemar had left the country while their fleets raided his coasts.

The Peace of Stralsund in 1370 gave the Hansa big trading rights and four castles in Skåne for 15 years. Valdemar came back and carried on ruling, a tough survivor to the end. When he died at Gurre in 1375 his sons were all dead. The crown would have to pass through one of his daughters.

claims.text: Valdemar set out three huge barrels in Visby's market and ordered the townsfolk to fill them with silver and gold.
claims.note: A Gotland tradition, made famous by Carl Gustaf Hellqvist's painting of 1882. No medieval source mentions the barrels.

claims.text: More than a thousand Gotland farmers died fighting outside Visby's walls in 1361.
claims.note: Archaeologists dug up mass graves at the battle site in 1905 and 1928–30. Many skeletons show terrible wounds, and some still wore their armour.

claims.text: Valdemar said God could keep heaven if he could keep Gurre, and now rides a ghostly hunt every night.
claims.note: A Danish folk legend recorded centuries later. Through J. P. Jacobsen's poems it inspired Schoenberg's Gurre-Lieder.

reigns.hook: Valdemar leaves two little grandsons with a claim. One is the son of his daughter Margaret and the King of Norway. Margaret is just 22, and she's about to outplay everyone.

reigns.tagline: The boy who wore two crowns and never got to use them
reigns.previously: Valdemar IV dies in 1375 with no sons left, only grandsons.
paragraphs: Two small boys had a claim. One was Albert of Mecklenburg, whose uncle was King of Sweden. The other was Olaf, son of Margaret and King Haakon VI of Norway. Margaret worked on the Danish nobles and bishops hard, and on 3 May 1376 they elected Olaf, aged five. Plenty of Danes were glad to avoid a king backed by the German princes of Mecklenburg.

Margaret ran Denmark in his name. When Haakon died in 1380, Olaf became King of Norway too, and through his father's family he had a claim to Sweden as well. His mother was getting ready to press it. Olaf grew up as heir to the whole of Scandinavia. Then, in August 1387, he died suddenly at Falsterbo Castle in Skåne, aged just 16.

claims.text: Olaf was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours went round, as they did whenever a young king died suddenly. There is no real evidence, and a fever is at least as likely.

claims.text: In 1402 a man turned up claiming to be Olaf, alive and well.
claims.note: The 'False Olaf' is well recorded. Margaret had his story checked, declared him a fraud and had him burned at Falsterbo.

reigns.hook: Olaf is dead and the royal line is empty. His mother isn't going anywhere. Within weeks the Danish nobles hand Margaret full power, and she means to keep it.

reigns.cameToPower: Given full power by the nobles
reigns.reignEnded: Died on her ship at Flensburg
reigns.previously: Teenage Olaf II dies suddenly at Falsterbo. No heir is left.
paragraphs: Margaret was Valdemar IV's daughter, married at ten to King Haakon of Norway. After her son died, the Danish nobles named her 'sovereign lady and master' with full power. Norway did the same early in 1388. Then she turned to Sweden, where the nobles were sick of their German king, Albert of Mecklenburg, and asked her for help.

Albert mocked her as a king without trousers. In 1389 her army beat his at Åsle and took him prisoner. Margaret now held all three kingdoms. To keep them together she adopted her sister's grandson, a Pomeranian boy whose name was changed to Eric. In 1397 she had him crowned at Kalmar as king of Denmark, Norway and Sweden. This was the Kalmar Union.

Eric was king in name, but Margaret ran everything until the day she died. She clawed back crown lands, kept the nobles in line and handled the Hansa with care. In October 1412 she fell ill on board her ship in Flensburg harbour and died. She was buried at Sorø and later moved to Roskilde Cathedral.

claims.text: Albert of Mecklenburg called her 'King Breechless' and sent her a whetstone to sharpen her needles.
claims.note: The insults come from later Swedish chronicle tradition. They fit Albert's reputation but can't be proved.

claims.text: Margaret was never crowned queen of Denmark in her own right.
claims.note: Her title was 'sovereign lady and master' and guardian of the realm. Margrethe II later took the numeral II in her honour all the same.

claims.text: The 1397 Union Letter was a binding treaty for the three kingdoms.
claims.note: The document survives on paper with only some of its seals. Historians still argue whether it was a final treaty or just a draft.

reigns.hook: Margaret is gone, and Eric finally has the three crowns all to himself. He's about 30, stubborn, and keen to show he never needed her.

reigns.tagline: The union king who ended up a pirate on Gotland
reigns.cameToPower: Took sole power at Margaret's death
reigns.previously: Margaret dies on her ship at Flensburg. Eric is on his own.
paragraphs: Eric had been king since boyhood, but with Margaret gone he finally called the shots. Back in 1406 he had married Philippa, daughter of Henry IV of England. He spent much of his reign fighting the Counts of Holstein over Schleswig, a long and costly war he never quite won.

His money idea was a hit. Around 1429 he started charging every ship that sailed through the Øresund past Helsingør. Those Sound Dues kept Danish kings rich for over 400 years. But his heavy taxes and foreign bailiffs were hated, and in 1434 the Swedish miners and farmers rose in revolt.

The Danish council turned on him too and deposed him in 1439. Eric holed up in Visborg Castle on Gotland with his treasure and lived by raiding Baltic shipping. Around 1449 he gave up and went home to Pomerania, where he lived quietly as a duke until his death in 1459.

claims.text: In exile Eric lived as a pirate king on Gotland.
claims.note: Hanseatic and Swedish records complain about ships seized by his men in the 1440s. 'Pirate' is his enemies' word, but the raids were real.

claims.text: Queen Philippa led the defence of Copenhagen against a Hanseatic fleet in 1428.
claims.note: Later chronicles give her the credit. How hands-on she really was is hard to know.

claims.text: Eric's push to make his cousin Bogislaw of Pomerania his heir helped turn the councils against him.
claims.note: The councils of all three kingdoms refused Bogislaw, and the row fed into his deposition.

reigns.hook: The council needs a new king fast. They choose Eric's own nephew, Christopher, a young prince from Bavaria with a royal mother and no track record at all.

reigns.tagline: The Bavarian who made Copenhagen the capital
reigns.cameToPower: Invited in by the Danish council
reigns.previously: Eric of Pomerania is deposed and sulking on Gotland.
paragraphs: Christopher was the son of Eric's sister Catherine and a Bavarian prince. The Danish council picked him because he was royal, foreign and, they hoped, easy to manage. He was elected in 1440, Sweden took him in 1441 and Norway in 1442. The union was back together, at least on paper.

His first test came from the farmers of north Jutland, who rose up in 1441. He crushed them in battle. He also made a lasting change: from 1443 the royal court settled in Copenhagen, and it has been the capital ever since. In 1445 he married Dorothea of Brandenburg.
In January 1448 he died suddenly at Helsingborg, aged 31, with no children. Once again the Danes had to go shopping for a king.

claims.text: In Sweden he was nicknamed the 'Bark King' because a famine forced the poor to mix bark into their bread.
claims.note: The nickname is in Swedish chronicles. Blaming the king for bad harvests says more about Swedish feelings for the union than about him.

claims.text: Copenhagen has been Denmark's capital since 1443.
claims.note: That is the year the royal court settled there. It's the standard date, though the shift was gradual.

reigns.hook: Christopher's young widow Dorothea comes with the job. The council's choice for king, and for her next husband, is a 22-year-old count from Oldenburg.

reigns.tagline: The broke king who pawned Shetland for a dowry
reigns.previously: Christopher of Bavaria dies at 31. No children, no heir.
paragraphs: Christian was a minor German count from Oldenburg. The council first offered the crown to his uncle, Duke Adolf of Schleswig, who said no and put forward his nephew. Christian was elected in 1448 and married Christopher's widow Dorothea. His family has held the Danish throne ever since, through one branch or another.

He took Norway in 1450 and Sweden in 1457, though the Swedes threw him out in 1464. In 1460 he was also chosen as Duke of Schleswig and Count of Holstein, with a promise that the two lands would stay together forever. That promise would start wars 400 years later.

He was always short of money. When his daughter Margaret married James III of Scotland, he couldn't pay the dowry, so he pledged Orkney in 1468 and Shetland in 1469 instead. Denmark never got them back. In 1479 he founded the University of Copenhagen, and two years later he died in the city.

claims.text: Orkney and Shetland were only pawned, so Denmark could still buy them back.
claims.note: Danish kings tried to redeem them more than once. Scotland annexed the islands in 1472 and never let the matter reopen.

claims.text: Christian promised that Schleswig and Holstein would stay 'forever undivided'.
claims.note: The phrase, 'up ewig ungedeelt' in Low German, comes from the Treaty of Ribe of 1460. Nineteenth-century nationalists made it a battle cry.

claims.text: He went to Rome in 1474 and got the Pope's blessing for a Danish university.
claims.note: The papal bull of 1475 is the founding charter. The university opened in 1479.

reigns.hook: Christian's son John takes over. The Swedes still won't play along, and down in the marshes of Dithmarschen some very stubborn farmers are waiting.

reigns.tagline: The king whose Black Guard drowned in the marshes
reigns.previously: Christian I dies in 1481. Orkney and Shetland are gone.
paragraphs: John was 26 when his father died, and the nobles made him sign a tough charter before they accepted him. He spent years trying to get Sweden back. In 1497 he finally beat the Swedes and was crowned in Stockholm. He held on for four years before they threw him out again.

His worst day came on 17 February 1500. John and his brother Frederick invaded Dithmarschen, a free farmers' republic on the North Sea coast, with a huge army that included the feared Black Guard mercenaries. At Hemmingstedt the farmers let the water in. In the flooded marsh the heavy army couldn't move, and thousands were cut down.
He did better at sea, building a proper royal fleet that's seen as the start of the Danish navy. In February 1513 he was thrown from his horse in Jutland and died soon after at Aalborg Castle.

claims.text: The Dithmarschers captured the Dannebrog at Hemmingstedt and kept it as a trophy.
claims.note: Dithmarschen tradition says the banner hung in their church until the Danes took it back in 1559. Nobody can prove it was the 'original' flag.

claims.text: His flagship Gribshunden caught fire and sank off Ronneby in 1495.
claims.note: The wreck lies off the Swedish coast and has been studied by archaeologists in recent years. The king was ashore when the fire broke out.

claims.text: The farmers opened the dykes on purpose to flood the battlefield.
claims.note: Accounts agree the marsh was flooded, but how much was planning and how much was the weather is still argued over.

reigns.hook: John's son Christian takes over. He's clever, ruthless and in love with a Dutch girl called Dyveke. Sweden is about to find out what he's capable of.

reigns.tagline: The king who drowned Stockholm in blood and lost it all
reigns.previously: King John dies after a riding accident. His son takes over.
paragraphs: Christian II was sharp, restless and quick to anger. While running Norway for his father he met Dyveke, a Dutch girl in Bergen, and he kept her as his mistress even after marrying Isabella, sister of the future Emperor Charles V. Dyveke's mother Sigbrit became his top adviser. When Dyveke died suddenly in 1517, Christian had a nobleman executed for supposedly poisoning her.

In 1520 he conquered Sweden and was crowned in Stockholm. Days later, in November, his men seized dozens of nobles and churchmen who had opposed him, branded them heretics and beheaded them in the main square. About 80 people died in the Stockholm Bloodbath. Sweden rose in revolt under a young noble called Gustav Vasa.

At home he backed townsmen and farmers against the nobles, and the nobles had had enough. In January 1523 the Jutland lords renounced him, and in April he sailed for the Netherlands. He came back in 1531, was lured into talks, and spent his last 27 years a prisoner at Sønderborg and Kalundborg.

claims.text: Pacing in his cell at Sønderborg, Christian wore a groove into a stone table with his thumb.
claims.note: A popular tale from later centuries, made famous by 19th-century painters. There's no evidence from his own time.

claims.text: Torben Oxe poisoned Dyveke.
claims.note: Oxe was convicted on the king's orders after a trial that was a farce. There was never any proof she was poisoned at all.

claims.text: Christian promised an amnesty to his Swedish enemies before the Bloodbath.
claims.note: He had pledged to forgive his opponents. Charging them with heresy, a church crime, was the way round his own promise.

reigns.hook: With Christian gone, the rebel nobles offer the crown to his uncle Frederick, Duke of Schleswig-Holstein. He's 51 and he's waited a long time.

reigns.tagline: The uncle who took his nephew's throne and locked him up
reigns.cameToPower: Offered the crown by rebel nobles
reigns.previously: Christian II flees to the Netherlands. The throne is empty.
paragraphs: Frederick was Christian I's younger son and had spent his life as Duke of Schleswig-Holstein. When the Jutland nobles turned on his nephew, they offered him the crown, and he had to sign a charter giving them big privileges in return. He liked his castle at Gottorp in Schleswig and spent little time in Denmark proper.

Sweden was gone for good. Gustav Vasa was elected king there in June 1523, and the Kalmar Union was finished in all but name. Frederick was also oddly relaxed about the new Lutheran ideas. He protected the preacher Hans Tausen and let Lutheranism spread, even though he had promised to defend the old Church.

In 1531 Christian II came back with an army to Norway. Frederick's side lured him into talks with a promise of safe conduct, then locked him up for good. Frederick died at Gottorp in April 1533. The council couldn't agree on who should follow him, and Denmark slid towards civil war.

claims.text: Christian II was promised safe conduct before he was locked up.
claims.note: The promise was given by Frederick's negotiators in 1532. Breaking it shocked even some of Frederick's allies.

claims.text: Frederick made Hans Tausen his chaplain in 1526 to shield him from the bishops.
claims.note: The appointment is recorded, and it let Tausen keep preaching Luther's ideas in Viborg.

reigns.hook: Frederick's eldest son Christian is a committed Lutheran, and the bishops won't have him. While they stall, Lübeck and a German count invade to bring back Christian II. Civil war is coming.

reigns.tagline: He won a civil war and made Denmark Lutheran
reigns.cameToPower: Elected in the middle of a civil war
reigns.previously: Frederick I dies. Denmark slides into civil war.
paragraphs: At 17 Christian was at the Diet of Worms in 1521 and saw Martin Luther stand up to the Emperor. He came away a convinced Lutheran, so the Catholic bishops blocked him when his father died. Then Lübeck and Count Christopher of Oldenburg invaded in the name of the jailed Christian II. Farmers and townsmen rose up too. This was the Count's Feud.

In July 1534 the frightened nobles of Jutland elected Christian king. His general Johan Rantzau stormed rebel Aalborg that December and broke the peasant army. Copenhagen held out under siege for a year before it gave in during July 1536. Christian had won, but he owed his soldiers a fortune.

He paid it the Lutheran way. In August 1536 he had the bishops arrested, took all their lands for the crown and made Denmark a Lutheran state. Luther's friend Johannes Bugenhagen came to crown him in 1537. Norway lost its own council and was ruled as part of Denmark. Christian died at Koldinghus on New Year's Day 1559.

claims.text: Christian saw Luther at the Diet of Worms in 1521.
claims.note: He was there with his family's party as a teenager. Lutheran writers later made much of the moment.

claims.text: Skipper Clement, leader of the peasant army, was executed after the war.
claims.note: He was captured and put to death at Viborg in 1536. His revolt had terrified the nobility.

claims.text: The bishops were arrested to pay off the army more than out of faith.
claims.note: Historians argue over the mix. Christian's beliefs were real, but the church lands also cleared his war debts.

reigns.hook: Christian's son Frederick inherits a rich, Protestant kingdom. His first move is revenge on the marshes of Dithmarschen, where his grandfather's army drowned in 1500.

reigns.tagline: The party king who built Hamlet's castle
reigns.previously: Christian III dies on New Year's Day 1559. The Reformation is done.
paragraphs: Frederick started with a score to settle. In 1559, months after taking the throne, he marched on Dithmarschen, the farmers' republic that had humiliated his family at Hemmingstedt, and conquered it in weeks. Then he picked a fight with Sweden. The Northern Seven Years' War dragged on from 1563 to 1570 and ended with nobody really winning.

He lost in love too. He wanted to marry Anne Hardenberg, a Danish noblewoman, but his family and the council wouldn't have it. In 1572 he married his 15-year-old cousin Sophie of Mecklenburg instead, and it turned out a happy match.

Peace made him rich, mostly from the Sound Dues. He spent it on Kronborg, a grand castle at Helsingør that Shakespeare would make famous as Elsinore. He gave the astronomer Tycho Brahe the island of Hven, where Tycho built the best observatory in Europe. Frederick drank hard, and he died in 1588 leaving a ten-year-old heir.

claims.text: Frederick drank himself to death.
claims.note: People at the time remarked on his heavy drinking, and many historians link it to his death. The illness itself isn't clearly recorded.

claims.text: Kronborg is the Elsinore of Hamlet.
claims.note: The play is set at Elsinore, which is Helsingør, and English actors are recorded at the Danish court in the 1580s.

claims.text: Tycho Brahe's pet elk died after drinking too much beer and falling down the stairs.
claims.note: The story comes from Pierre Gassendi's life of Tycho, written decades later. It's too good to check, and nobody can.

reigns.tagline: Sixty years, a hundred buildings and one lost eye
reigns.previously: Frederick II is dead. His heir, Christian, is only ten.
paragraphs: Christian was ten when his father died, so a council of nobles ran Denmark until his coronation in 1596. Then he got busy. He built like a man possessed: Rosenborg Castle, the Stock Exchange, the Round Tower, a whole new district called Christianshavn and fresh towns across the realm, including Kristiania in Norway. He loved ships, music and women, and fathered a small crowd of children.

War was his weak spot. He beat Sweden in the Kalmar War of 1611–13, then jumped into the Thirty Years' War. In 1626 Tilly smashed his army at Lutter, and imperial troops overran Jutland. Against Sweden again in 1644, he was hit by flying splinters at the sea battle of Kolberger Heide and lost his right eye, yet kept directing the fight. The peace of 1645 still cost Denmark Gotland, Ösel, two Norwegian provinces and, for thirty years, Halland.

He reigned for almost 60 years, the longest of any Danish king. By the end, money was gone and the nobles were in charge of the bills. His eldest son and heir had died in 1647, so the crown passed to a second son nobody had planned on.

claims.text: Wounded and bleeding, Christian stood by the mast at Kolberger Heide and refused to leave the deck.
claims.note: Eyewitness reports and his own diary record the wound. The scene became the opening of the royal anthem 'Kong Christian stod ved højen mast'.

claims.text: Splinters taken from his face were turned into earrings for his mistress.
claims.note: A favourite tour-guide story. The fragments were kept, but the earring detail is hard to trace back to a reliable early source.

claims.text: He personally designed many of his buildings.
claims.note: He was closely involved and sketched plans, but architects such as Hans van Steenwinckel did most of the real design work.

reigns.tagline: Lost half the map, then took all the power
reigns.cameToPower: Elected after signing a strict charter
reigns.previously: Christian IV dies after 60 years; his eldest son is already dead.
paragraphs: Frederick only got the crown after promising the nobles nearly everything. He bided his time. In 1657 he declared war on Sweden, hoping to win back old losses. Instead, in the bitter winter of 1658, Charles X Gustav marched his army across the frozen sea straits to Zealand. At Roskilde that February Denmark gave up Skåne, Halland, Blekinge and more. The east side of the Sound has been Swedish ever since.

Months later Charles came back to finish the job. Copenhagen was besieged, and Frederick stayed in the city with its people. On a February night in 1659 the Swedes stormed the walls and were thrown back. The peace of 1660 returned Bornholm, and the king came out a hero.

He used that moment. In October 1660 the burghers and clergy, sick of the nobles, helped make the crown hereditary and the king absolute. The King's Law of 1665 spelled it out: the monarch answered only to God. Frederick passed that unlimited power to his son Christian.

claims.text: Frederick said he would 'die in his nest' rather than flee besieged Copenhagen.
claims.note: The line is widely quoted and fits his conduct, but the wording comes down through later retellings.

claims.text: The Swedish army walked across the frozen Belts to invade Zealand in 1658.
claims.note: One of the best documented feats of the era. Two cavalry squadrons were lost through the ice on the Little Belt.

claims.text: The King's Law was kept secret for decades.
claims.note: It was signed in 1665 but only printed and made public in 1709.

reigns.hook: Denmark now has the most absolute monarchy in Europe, on paper at least. Frederick's son Christian inherits it, along with a burning grudge against Sweden.

reigns.tagline: The absolute king who rode, hunted and wrote the law
reigns.cameToPower: First king born to absolute power
reigns.previously: Frederick III dies, leaving his son unlimited power.
paragraphs: Christian V was the first Danish king to inherit absolute power outright, and he enjoyed the show. He created counts and barons loyal to the crown and sat for an equestrian statue on Kongens Nytorv. For a while his clever chancellor Griffenfeld ran the government. In 1676 Griffenfeld was arrested for treason and sentenced to death, then spared on the scaffold and sent to prison for over twenty years.

Christian wanted Skåne back. In the Scanian War of 1675–79 the admiral Niels Juel crushed the Swedes at Køge Bay in 1677, but on land the bloody battle of Lund went badly. The great powers made the peace, and Denmark won nothing.

His lasting work was the Danish Law of 1683, one code for the whole kingdom, with a Norwegian version in 1687. In 1698 he was hurt in a hunting accident and never fully recovered. He died the next summer, and his son Frederick took over.

claims.text: Griffenfeld was pardoned at the very last moment, with the axe ready.
claims.note: The reprieve on the scaffold in 1676 is well recorded. His sentence was turned into life imprisonment.

claims.text: Parts of the Danish Law of 1683 stayed in force for centuries.
claims.note: Some of its sections are still technically valid today, which legal historians like to point out.

reigns.hook: Christian is dead. His son Frederick is 27, restless, and looking for a war to undo his father's failures. He'll also find a startling number of wives.

reigns.tagline: Fought Sweden for twenty years and married three times
reigns.previously: Christian V dies after a hunting accident.
paragraphs: Frederick IV went to war almost at once. In 1700 he joined the attack on Sweden, but the young Charles XII landed near Copenhagen and forced Denmark out within months. Frederick tried again in 1709, after Charles's army was wrecked in Russia. A defeat at Helsingborg in 1710 ended dreams of Skåne, but the naval hero Tordenskjold kept the Swedes busy. The peace of 1720 gave Denmark the Gottorp lands in Schleswig.

At home he was more interesting. While still married to Queen Louise, he took a second wife in 1703, then a third, Anna Sophie Reventlow, in 1712, after carrying her off from her family's manor. When Louise died in 1721 he crowned Anna Sophie queen, to the fury of his son. He sent missionaries to India and Greenland and built Fredensborg, the palace of peace. He died in 1730 and his son Christian came in hungry for revenge on his stepmother.

claims.text: Frederick 'abducted' Anna Sophie Reventlow from Clausholm.
claims.note: Her family were horrified, but she seems to have gone willingly. The 'abduction' was more like an elopement.

claims.text: He was married to two women at the same time, with the Church's quiet blessing.
claims.note: Both later marriages were made while Queen Louise was still alive, and are well recorded.

reigns.hook: Frederick is dead, and Queen Anna Sophie is suddenly alone. His son Christian, pious and stiff, can't stand her. Out she goes, and in comes a very sober court.

reigns.tagline: The pious king who shut down the theatre
reigns.previously: Frederick IV dies; Christian loathes his stepmother.
paragraphs: Christian VI was a devout Pietist, and his court felt like a church. He banished his stepmother Anna Sophie to her family's manor at Clausholm. Then he made religion a duty for everyone: compulsory church on Sundays, and from 1736 confirmation for every young Dane. Comedy was seen as sinful, so the theatre in Copenhagen was shut and actors had to find other work.

He wasn't shy about spending, though. He tore down the old Copenhagen Castle and started the first Christiansborg Palace, a vast baroque pile. He also built Hirschholm and the Hermitage hunting lodge. In 1733 a law tied young farmhands to the estate where they were born, a bond that lasted over 50 years. Denmark stayed at peace. In 1746 Christian died, and his fun-loving son Frederick threw the theatre doors back open.

claims.text: Christian VI banned theatre performances in Denmark.
claims.note: Comedies were suppressed during his reign. Holberg's famous theatre had closed in 1728 and could not reopen under him.

claims.text: The first Christiansborg burned down only about fifty years after it was finished.
claims.note: The palace was destroyed by fire in 1794.

reigns.hook: Christian is dead. His son Frederick is 23, charming, and likes parties far better than prayers. He'll leave Copenhagen a gorgeous new district and a drinking problem.

reigns.tagline: A golden age built while the king drank
reigns.previously: Pious Christian VI dies; his son likes a party.
paragraphs: Frederick V was popular and pleasant and didn't work too hard. Able ministers like Moltke and Bernstorff did that for him. Under them Denmark had a cultural boom. The theatre came back, an Academy of Fine Arts opened, and a grand new district, Frederiksstaden, was laid out in Copenhagen. Its heart was Amalienborg, four palaces round an octagon, where the royal family still lives.

The government also kept Denmark out of the Seven Years' War, and paid for a famous scientific trip to Arabia in 1761. Only one member, Carsten Niebuhr, came home alive. The king himself drank heavily, and it wore him down. His first queen, Louise, died in 1751. He died in 1766 aged just 42, leaving the crown to his son Christian, sixteen and very fragile.

claims.text: Frederick V spent much of his reign drunk.
claims.note: Courtiers and foreign diplomats wrote about it openly. His heavy drinking is accepted by his biographers.

claims.text: The gilded statue in the middle of Amalienborg cost more than all four palaces around it.
claims.note: A popular claim. The French sculptor Saly's statue of Frederick was very expensive, but the comparison depends on how you count.

reigns.hook: Frederick is dead at 42. His son Christian is sixteen, handsome and clearly unwell. Within a few years a German doctor will be running the country.

reigns.tagline: The mad king, his doctor and his queen
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Rendsburg; long in name only
reigns.previously: Frederick V drinks himself to an early grave.
paragraphs: Christian VII was sixteen and already in trouble. He was mentally ill and could barely do his job. He married Caroline Matilda, sister of Britain's George III, then ignored her. On a tour of Europe in 1768 he picked up a German doctor, Johann Friedrich Struensee, who could calm him down. Back home, Struensee became the king's best friend, the queen's lover and, by 1770, the real ruler of Denmark.

Struensee issued over a thousand orders in barely sixteen months. He ended press censorship and cut court spending. Enemies at court hated him. In January 1772 the king's stepmother staged a coup. Struensee was beheaded and quartered, the queen was divorced and sent away to Celle, where she died at 23.
In 1784 Christian's son Frederick, sixteen, took control of the council and ran Denmark as regent for the next 24 years. The old king lived on in a fog until 1808.

claims.text: Struensee was the real father of the queen's daughter, Louise Augusta.
claims.note: It was whispered at court and widely believed, but there is no proof. She was officially the king's child.

claims.text: Christian VII suffered from schizophrenia.
claims.note: Modern writers often suggest it, but diagnosing someone dead for two centuries is guesswork.

claims.text: Struensee issued more than a thousand decrees in about sixteen months.
claims.note: His orders survive in the archives. Historians count them in the high hundreds to well over a thousand.

reigns.hook: The old king is dead at last. His son Frederick has run Denmark for years already. Now he's king in name too, and Britain has just burned his capital.

reigns.tagline: The king who lost the fleet, the money and Norway
reigns.previously: Mad Christian VII dies after 42 years as king in name.
paragraphs: Frederick had already been running Denmark for years. As regent he ended the bond that tied farmhands to their estates, in 1788. Then the Napoleonic wars swallowed him. In September 1807 a British fleet bombarded Copenhagen for three nights to stop the Danish navy falling to Napoleon. Much of the city burned, and the British sailed off with the whole fleet. Furious, Frederick stuck with France.

It was a ruinous bet. In 1813 the state went bankrupt. When Napoleon collapsed, Denmark was on the losing side, and the Treaty of Kiel in 1814 handed Norway to Sweden after 400 years of union. Somehow Frederick stayed popular, a plain, fatherly figure. In the 1830s he set up advisory assemblies, a first small taste of having a say. He had no surviving sons, so the crown went to his cousin, the prince who had once been king of Norway.

claims.text: The British bombardment of 1807 was one of the first deliberate attacks on a city's civilians.
claims.note: Some historians describe it that way. Others say the Congreve rockets and shells aimed at the defences simply hit homes.

claims.text: Denmark lost Norway in 1814 after more than four centuries together.
claims.note: The Treaty of Kiel, signed in January 1814, gave Norway to the king of Sweden.

reigns.hook: Frederick dies without sons. Next up is his cousin Christian, who once gave Norway a constitution. Liberals are sure he'll give Denmark one too.

reigns.tagline: Once a rebel king of Norway, then a careful one at home
reigns.previously: Frederick VI dies with no son; his cousin inherits.
paragraphs: In 1814 young Prince Christian Frederik was governor of Norway when it was handed to Sweden. He refused to accept it. A Norwegian assembly at Eidsvoll wrote one of Europe's most liberal constitutions, signed on 17 May, and chose him as king. Sweden invaded. After a short war he gave up the throne in October and went home to Denmark.

Liberals expected him to bring the same freedoms to Denmark when he became king at 53. He didn't. He was clever, cultured and keen on science, but he kept absolute power. He did loosen the rules on local government and in his last weeks he seems to have accepted change was coming. He died in January 1848, weeks before revolutions swept Europe. His son Frederick had to face them.

claims.text: He was king of Norway for less than five months.
claims.note: Elected on 17 May 1814, he abdicated on 10 October 1814 after the war with Sweden.

claims.text: On his deathbed he told his son to grant a constitution.
claims.note: Often repeated. He was moving in that direction, but the deathbed advice comes from later tellings.

reigns.hook: Christian is dead, and 1848 is about to explode. His son Frederick is a heavy-drinking, warm-hearted oddball. A crowd is heading for the palace.

reigns.tagline: The king who gave away his own power
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Glücksburg, last of his line
reigns.previously: Christian VIII dies as revolution brews.
paragraphs: Frederick VII was nobody's idea of a model king. He drank, told tall tales and had two failed marriages behind him. But in March 1848, when a huge crowd marched on Christiansborg, he simply agreed to change. He said he now saw himself as a constitutional king. On 5 June 1849 he signed Denmark's first constitution, with an elected parliament. Absolute monarchy was over after 189 years.

Danes loved him for it. They also put up with his third wife, Louise Rasmussen, a former ballet dancer whom he made Countess Danner. High society sneered. Frederick didn't care. He dug up ancient burial mounds for fun, too. Meanwhile war over Schleswig was fought from 1848 to 1851. He had no children, and the great powers picked a distant relative, Prince Christian of Glücksburg, as heir. Frederick died in 1863 just as the Schleswig crisis boiled over.

claims.text: Frederick VII 'gave' Denmark its constitution freely.
claims.note: That's the popular memory. In fact he gave in to pressure from crowds and politicians in 1848, though he went along with good grace.

claims.text: Countess Danner was a former dancer and milliner's apprentice.
claims.note: Louise Rasmussen trained at the Royal Theatre's ballet school and later ran a fashion shop, which the nobility never let her forget.

reigns.hook: The last Oldenburg king is dead. On the new king's desk sits a constitution tying Schleswig closer to Denmark. Sign it and Prussia attacks.
