reigns.tagline: Lost the duchies, married his children to Europe
reigns.previously: Frederick VII, last of the old line, dies childless.
paragraphs: Christian IX's reign began with a disaster. Days after taking the throne he signed the November Constitution, which bound Schleswig to Denmark. Prussia and Austria invaded. On 18 April 1864 the Prussians stormed the redoubts at Dybbøl. By October Denmark had lost Schleswig, Holstein and Lauenburg. It was the country's darkest hour, and many blamed the German-born king.

His family made up for it. His daughter Alexandra married the future Edward VII of Britain. Another, Dagmar, became Empress of Russia. His son George became King of the Hellenes, and his grandson became Haakon VII of Norway. Every summer the clan gathered at Fredensborg. At home he fought parliament for decades, but in 1901 he accepted a government backed by the majority. He died at 87, and his son Frederick took over at 62.

claims.text: He was called 'the father-in-law of Europe'.
claims.note: The nickname was used in his own lifetime, with good reason: his children married into the royal houses of Britain, Russia and Greece.

claims.text: Christian was chosen as heir because of his wife's bloodline.
claims.note: His wife Louise of Hesse-Kassel was a niece of Christian VIII and had the stronger claim. She passed her rights to him.

reigns.reignEnded: Collapsed on a street in Hamburg
reigns.previously: Christian IX dies at 87 after 42 years.
paragraphs: Frederick VIII had been crown prince for longer than most people live. He was more liberal than his father and got on well with parliament. Just before he became king, his son Carl was chosen as King of Norway and took the name Haakon VII. Frederick's own reign was short and quiet.

In May 1912 he was coming home from a holiday in Nice and stopped in Hamburg. He went out alone for an evening walk, without anyone knowing who he was. He collapsed in the street and died. He was taken to a hospital as an unknown man, and only identified later. His son Christian, already 41, became king.

claims.text: Frederick died in Hamburg after slipping out for a walk incognito.
claims.note: Newspapers at the time reported it.

claims.text: He collapsed near a brothel.
claims.note: This rumour has circulated for a century. There is no solid evidence for it, and the royal family never acknowledged it.

reigns.hook: Frederick is dead. His son Christian is tall, stiff and stubborn. He'll nearly lose his crown in a row with parliament, then become a symbol of defiance.

reigns.tagline: The king on horseback in occupied Copenhagen
reigns.previously: Frederick VIII collapses unknown in a Hamburg street.
paragraphs: Christian X nearly wrecked the monarchy in 1920. He sacked an elected government during a row over Schleswig. Crowds rioted, unions threatened a general strike, and talk turned to a republic. He backed down in days. That summer North Schleswig voted to rejoin Denmark, and he rode across the old border on a white horse. Iceland, meanwhile, became a separate kingdom under him in 1918, and a republic in 1944.

In April 1940 Germany occupied Denmark. Christian kept riding through Copenhagen every morning, alone, and Danes took heart from it. In 1942 Hitler sent him a long birthday telegram. The king's curt reply made Hitler livid. Weeks later Christian was badly hurt in a riding fall and never recovered. He lived to see liberation in 1945. His son Frederick took over in 1947.

claims.text: Christian threatened to wear the yellow star if the Nazis made Danish Jews wear it.
claims.note: Denmark never had a yellow star decree. The story spread after the war, though it fits his attitude.

claims.text: His one-line reply to Hitler's birthday telegram caused a diplomatic crisis in 1942.
claims.note: The 'Telegram Crisis' is well documented. Hitler recalled his envoy and demanded a tougher government in Copenhagen.

claims.text: He rode alone through Copenhagen each day during the occupation.
claims.note: Photographs and many witnesses confirm it. He did it before the war too.

reigns.tagline: The tattooed sailor king who changed the rules
reigns.previously: Christian X dies two years after liberation.
paragraphs: Frederick IX had served in the navy and came back with tattoos, including a dragon. He was relaxed, friendly and loved music. He sometimes conducted the Royal Danish Orchestra himself, and recordings survive. With his Swedish queen, Ingrid, he made the monarchy feel modern and close.

There was one snag. He had three daughters and no sons, and the law said only men could inherit. The heir was his brother Knud. In 1953 a new constitution and a new act of succession let a woman take the throne if she had no brothers. Danes voted for it. His eldest daughter, Margrethe, became heir at 13. He died in January 1972 after a short illness.

claims.text: Frederick IX had several tattoos from his navy days.
claims.note: Photographs show them. Tattoos were a sailor's tradition, and he made no secret of his.

claims.text: He conducted the Royal Danish Orchestra on records.
claims.note: Several recordings of him conducting were released.

reigns.tagline: The artist queen who reigned for 52 years
reigns.reignEnded: Abdicated in favour of her son
reigns.previously: Frederick IX dies; his daughter is first in line.
paragraphs: Margrethe II was proclaimed queen from the balcony of Christiansborg Palace by the prime minister. She was the first female ruler since Margaret I in the 1400s. She had studied at universities in Denmark, Cambridge, Paris and London, and was a keen archaeologist. In 1967 she married a French diplomat, Henri de Laborde de Monpezat, who became Prince Henrik. They had two sons, Frederik and Joachim.

She was also a serious artist. Under the pen name Ingahild Grathmer she illustrated a Danish edition of The Lord of the Rings in 1977. She designed costumes and sets for ballets, plays and films. Her reign lasted 52 years. On New Year's Eve 2023, in her live televised speech, she surprised the nation by announcing she would step down. She signed her abdication on 14 January 2024, and her son became king that day.

claims.text: She was the first Danish queen to reign in her own right since Margaret I.

reigns.tagline: The frogman, marathon runner and king
reigns.previously: Margrethe II signs her abdication after 52 years.
paragraphs: Frederik X was proclaimed king on 14 January 2024 by prime minister Mette Frederiksen from the balcony of Christiansborg Palace. Huge crowds filled the square. He chose a motto: United, committed, for the Kingdom of Denmark.

He trained hard for the job, in his own way. He studied political science at Aarhus University and served in the armed forces, passing the gruelling training of the navy's elite frogman corps. He has run marathons and crossed northern Greenland by dog sled. In 2000 he met Mary Donaldson, an Australian, in Sydney during the Olympic Games. They married in 2004 and have four children. Their eldest, Christian, is now crown prince.

claims.note: Both have told the story publicly. They met at the Slip Inn in Sydney.
